title: Indifference is not equanimity

lines: A CALM THAT IS A CLOSED DOOR.
cards: Someone tells you their bad news, and you say, well, whatever happens, happens. It sounds calm. It might even sound wise.
But look at the person across the table. They came to you, and you shrugged. There's a kind of calm that is really a closed door: I'm fine because I've stopped caring.
An old Buddhist manual saw that this shrug can pass for the real thing, and gave it a name, and a warning.

teach.b: By now the map is familiar.

In Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification, each of the four immeasurables has two enemies: a far one, the plain opposite, and a near one that looks like the quality, stands close to it, and quietly takes its place.
You've met two near enemies already: clinging dressed up as kindness, and sorrow dressed up as compassion, with pity as its modern cousin.
For equanimity, the near enemy is what Buddhaghosa calls the equanimity of unknowing: the dull, blank indifference of someone who simply hasn't looked.
Its far enemies are greed and resentment, the pull toward and the push away. So real equanimity sits in a narrow place. It isn't grabbing, it isn't pushing, and it isn't numb.
It sees clearly, it cares, and it doesn't lose its footing.
The Dhammapada has a picture for this, in Max Müller's translation: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." A rock in the wind is not asleep.
The wind is real, and it hits the rock. It just isn't knocked over. That's the test.
Indifference turns away so it won't be moved.
Equanimity turns toward, lets itself be touched, and stays standing. The first protects you from other people. The second lets you stay with them, even when you can't fix what's wrong.

how: Buddhist teachers often introduce the near and far enemies of the four immeasurables as a way to check one's practice honestly; equanimity is usually cultivated last, after kindness, compassion and gladness, so that it rests on warmth rather than distance.

o: calm that still cares and keeps its footing
calm that comes from no longer caring
a balance reached by avoiding strong feelings

games.q: match each quality to its near enemy.
p: not shaken by blame and praise

s: equanimity means not caring what happens
not caring is its near enemy; equanimity cares and keeps its footing.
Buddhaghosa gives each immeasurable a near enemy and a far enemy
the near enemy looks alike; the far enemy is the plain opposite.
equanimity's far enemies are greed and resentment
the pull toward and the push away.

games.q: a friend tells you their marriage is ending. you can't fix it. which response is equanimity?
o: 'these things happen,' and change the subject.
stay, listen, feel it with them, and don't pretend you can fix it.
take on their pain as your own until you can't sleep.
games.why: the first is the shrug, the near enemy. the third loses footing. equanimity stays close and stays standing.

practice: Let sounds and sensations come like wind against a rock, a car outside, an itch, a thought about later, and feel each one arrive without shutting it out or chasing it.
Then bring to mind one person in trouble and let the care come in like one more gust: felt fully, touched but not knocked over. Rest as the rock, open to the wind.

wordCard.voice: Upekkhā. Equanimity, literally looking on from close by: the shrug that stops caring is its near enemy, while real equanimity cares and still stands.

orig.note: Pali upekkhā: equanimity, literally 'looking on' from close by, not from far away.

carryVoice: Your line: care, then let go. A rock in the wind, not a closed door. That's day two hundred forty-one.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
sources.q: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.
